Unlike the enduring stars, we wither; unlike the timeless hills and cisterns, we perish. Ana stood in the shadow of my protector, the esteemed Arbad, who has now departed from us. Yet Ana does not grieve, for every sparrow must eventually fly forth from the feast hall. Novelties no longer excite me, nor do *wyrdstaef* affright me. 

Men are like temporary encampments that swiftly crumble into ruins. They arrive alongside their kin, leaving behind only bare earth when they depart—like the last herdsman gathering the stragglers. Man is but a shooting star: brilliance turned to ash. Wealth and kin are merely stains destined to wear away, and the work of our hands inevitably becomes *gehrorene*. The wise grasp this truth; the foolish fight against it, only to lose. If my *wyrd* grants a brief reprieve, my fingers still reach out to grasp its staff. Ana can tell you stories, bending ever lower the more I strive to stand tall. Ana am like a battle-battered sword—worn, yet no less sharp. Do not leave me! *(And suddenly, the sparrow finds the exit—)*

O you reproachful *wifcynn*: when the men march off, can your witchcraft truly reveal who shall return? Do you faint because they *flet ofgeāfon*—deserted the hall? You move all to tears, weeping over the broken bodies of the irreplaceable friends of your youth! Yet neither witches nor necromancers know what the *ælmihtig* intends. Demand of them: *Hwær cōm* the men? *Hwær cōm* our protectors? They cannot even foretell when the rainstorm will fall!

***

### The Inevitable Horizon: Reflections on Mortality, Wisdom, and Fate

The overarching narrative of human existence is fundamentally marked by transience. No matter how grand our accomplishments, how vast our accumulated wealth, or how vibrant our lives may seem in their prime, all are subject to the relentless march of time. Empires crumble into dust, treasures lose their luster, and the physical manifestations of human ambition inevitably decay. To pretend that our earthly creations are permanent is to ignore the foundational law of the natural world: everything that rises must eventually fall.

Faced with this inexorable reality, the true measure of human character comes to light. Wisdom lies not in attempting to conquer mortality, but in quietly accepting it alongside the dictates of fate. The foolish waste their brief days fighting an unwinnable war against destiny, raging against the dying of the light and clinging to illusions of control. Conversely, the wise recognize that peace is found in surrender—not a surrender of purpose, but an acceptance of limits. By embracing our finitude, we free ourselves from the anxiety of trying to outrun time.

While time unquestionably claims the physical body, its reach over the human spirit is limited. Old age may wear down the frame, slow the stride, and dim the physical senses, but it does not possess the inherent power to dull a person’s inner strength or mental sharpness. Indeed, as the outer shell deteriorates, the interior life often grows more luminous. Fortified by decades of experience, a resilient mind and a steeled soul can remain untouched by the physical frailties of aging, proving that true vigor belongs to the spirit rather than the flesh.

In their desperation to escape mortality or pierce the veil of the unknown, humans have often turned to the dark arts and mystic arts. Yet, these pursuits offer only false promises. Neither witches nor necromancers, despite their claims of supernatural mastery, possess the sight to discern divine intentions or foretell the ultimate fate of fallen warriors. The final destination of a departed soul and the grand design of the cosmos remain entirely beyond the reach of sorcery. The mysteries of life and death are governed by a higher power, forever shielded from mortal arrogance and occult intrigue.

Ultimately, no degree of philosophy or spiritual resolve can completely insulate us from the pain of living. The loss of irreplaceable friends, mentors, and protectors brings a profound and heavy grief—a sorrow that honors the depth of our connection to them. Yet, even in the depths of mourning, we are reminded of the universal truth that binds us all: death is the inescapable outcome for every living soul. In recognizing that our fallen comrades have merely answered the same summons that awaits us all, we find the strength to endure our grief, walking forward with quiet dignity toward our own inevitable horizon.

Here is the expanded text, written in an elevated, elegiac style that draws directly upon the atmospheric and philosophical tradition of Old English poetry.

***

### The Winter of the World

Under a leaden, snow-heavy sky, where the cold sea lashes against the barren rock, a lone voice speaks into the gale. He is a solitary survivor of a forgotten time, a wanderer walking through a world grown dim and cold. As the frost binds the earth and the wind howls through the hollow ruins of once-great stone halls, he delivers his solemn lamentation—a meditation on the fleeting nature of all earthly creation.

Where now are the joy and the laughter that once echoed through the meadhall? Where is the ring-giver, the noble lord who draped his loyal warriors in gold and granted them land and protection? The grave has swallowed them all. The great timbered halls, once vibrant with song, harp-strumming, and the clinking of ale-horns, now stand as desolate, wind-swept ghosts draped in ivy and snow. The death of the protector leaves the solitary man stripped of his home and purpose, casting him out into the bitter wilderness of exile. Through this ruin, the speaker sees the true face of the world: a place where glory is merely a passing shadow, and every earthly haven eventually crumbles into dust.

This decay is not merely woven into the earth, but etched into the very flesh of humanity. The speaker reflects on the relentless advance of time upon the mortal body. Youth, with its bright eyes, swift limbs, and bold arrogance, is an illusion that shatters all too quickly. Strength inevitably bows to the stoop of age; the dark hair turns to frost, the hands tremble, and the memory grows thin like winter ice. No warrior, regardless of his past valor or the number of battles fought, can slay the slow, creeping specter of senility. Death awaits both the king on his throne and the churl in his hut; the grave is the final, equalizing home for all who draw breath beneath the heavens.

In their desperation to escape this grim certainty, men turn to every desperate remedy available to them. They build high fortresses with thick stone walls, hoping to hoard their breath behind barricades of granite. They gather mountains of gold, mistaking wealth for an armor against the grave. Others, driven by fear, venture into the dark and turn to forbidden arts. They whisper ancient runic incantations, brew potions of root and bone, and invoke the uncanny forces of witchcraft to peer into the unknown or turn away the pale hand of death. 

Yet, the speaker warns, all these efforts are reduced to folly in the end. The sorcerer dies alongside the king; the witch’s chant is choked out by the same soil that fills the mouths of the simple-minded. No mortal cunning, no earthly iron, and no dark magic can unbind the threads woven by the divine sovereign. Divine fate—*Wyrd*—moves according to a design that no human eye can foresee and no mortal power can alter. To believe that one can outsmart or outfight the divine order through witchcraft or strength is the ultimate arrogance of the fool.

True wisdom, therefore, begins not in resistance, but in stillness and understanding. The wise man does not weep uncontrollably for the fallen hall, nor does he waste his brief days seeking spells to stretch out his fleeting life. Instead, he looks upon the transience of the world with a quiet, patient heart. He accepts that all earthly treasure is borrowed, that every joy is fleeting, and that humanity is merely passing through a dark, wintery night toward an eternal judgment. By relinquishing the foolish fight against impermanence, the soul finds its only true peace, submitting humbly to the higher power that governs the end of all things.

In the quiet valley between the misty northern hills, **Ana** had spent years listening to the legends of the old forge. The elders spoke of **Arbad**, a master blacksmith whose steel was said to be so pure it could catch the fading light of the stars. Many travelers had sought his workshop over the decades, hoping to commission weapons of unmatched strength, **but** Arbad had long since retired from the craft, preferring the solace of his garden and the gentle rhythm of a quiet life.

When **Ana** finally reached his small stone cottage, she did not carry iron or gold. Instead, she brought a single broken compass—an heirloom from her grandfather that no ordinary artisan had been able to repair. **Arbad** examined the intricate, rusted gears and initially shook his head, insisting his anvil had been cold for a decade. **But** as Ana turned to leave, the setting sun struck the brass casing, illuminating a hidden inscription etched into the metal by a hand he recognized all too well.

Without another word, the old smith gestured for her to step inside and unlocked the door to his long-dormant workshop. That evening, the rhythmic strike of a hammer on hot iron echoed through the valley once more, rekindling a forgotten legacy that neither of them had expected to revive.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an elegiac prose poem inspired by Old English poetry like *The Wanderer*. Incorporate Bede's sparrow-in-the-hall motif, the *ubi sunt* motif, and blend modern English with authentic Old English vocabulary such as *wyrd*, *wifcynn*, and *aelmihtig*.
counterfactuals.output:
Lone stands the *eardstapa* upon the rim of a grey world, where the salt-waves lash the bone-white cliffs and the rime-frost glazes the fallen timber. He folds his arms over his chest, keeping fast the lock-box of his spirit, for the wise man knows that sorrow must be bound in silence, held secret behind the wall of teeth. All is bleak across this twilight *middangeard*, driven by biting gales that sweep the high hills. No warrior can outrun the wheel of time, for untamed and unyielding is *wyrd*, shaping the destinies of men beneath the brooding sky.

I recall the high-gabled *meduseld*, its timbered walls humming with song, warm with the red glow of peat and oak. Outside, the night was vast and hostile, a wilderness of winter-sorrow and blind snow. And as the men drank their sweet mead, a sparrow darted into the hall, flying in through one open door. For a brief, shining moment, it knew the heat of the hearth-fire, the smell of roasting meats, and the safe comfort of the bench-boards, untouched by the winter storm. But then, passing through the fire-light, it flew out the other door, vanishing back into the freezing dark from whence it came. So too is the life of man: a momentary fluttering through a brightly lit room, bounded on either side by an unknown, icy shadow.

Where now has the horse gone? Where is the young warrior? Where is the *goldwine*, the beloved lord who once showered rings and amber into open palms? Hwær cwom the sound of the harp? Hwær cwom the bright feast-goblets and the laughter of the hearth-companions? All have vanished into the gullet of time, swallowed as if they had never been. The giant-built stone walls crumble into moss, stripped of their roofs, exposed to the flaying wind. Where now is the tender *wifcynn*, whose gentle words lulled the battle-weary to sleep and whose kin wove peace between warring clans? The dust has claimed them all; glory turns to ash, and bright joy falls into grey evening.

The world grows old and falters, its ancient strength leaking into the frost. Yet the solitary traveller does not curse the cold, nor does he weep for the stone halls that have tumbled into dust. He surrenders his longing to the grey sea and looks beyond the broken ruins of this fleeting earth, seeking comfort in the eternal, unshakeable strength of the *aelmihtig*, where no lord dies, no hall collapses, and the winter storm can never enter.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dramatic monologue from the perspective of an aging Anglo-Saxon elder named Ana who is reflecting on mortality, fallen warriors, and the inscrutable nature of fate.
counterfactuals.output:
*(The stage is dark save for the dull red embers of a dying hearth fire. ANA sits wrapped in a heavy, grease-stained wool cloak, her gnarled, dirt-caked fingers tracing the rusty links of a scrap of mail-armor. Her voice is like stones grinding together, slow and raspy, but carrying the resonant weight of survival.)*

Blow upon the ash, old breath… see if a single spark remains. 

There is little heat left in these sodden turfs, and less within this crumbling bone-house of mine. Look at these fingers. Like the frozen roots of an elder-tree, clawing at dirt that remembers none of my youth. 

They are all gone into the earth-grip. All of them. 

*(She shakes her head, a soft, dry laugh rattling in her chest.)*

Where are the ring-givers now? Where are the proud thains who swore over silver-hilted blades that they would fell the sea-wolves or die upon the sward? I remember the morning at the river-ford. The dawn broke red as fresh-spilled wine. I saw young Cynewulf—his hair bright as beaten copper—raise his lime-wood shield against the gray sky. He laughed! The fool sang to the cold morning air as if death were a maiden waiting in the high hall.

By noon, the ravens were feasting on his eyes. The wolf, that greedy dawn-flyer, tore the meat from his thighs while the blood was yet warm enough to steam in the moss. 

I washed the red mud from his brow before we laid him in the barrow. His flesh was hard and smooth as polished horn. And I… I was already old then. Yet here I sit, a hollowed reed left standing in the frost, while the oak trees have all been felled. 

Why? Tell me that, you dark stars through the smoke-hole! Tell me the measure of it!

*(She leans forward, gripping the scrap of mail tighter, her eyes glittering in the ember-light.)*

*Wyrd* weaves as she wills. That is the only truth left to a woman who has buried three sons and a husband under the cold turf. Fate is a blind weaver sitting in the shadows. She pulls the silver thread—the strong, the beautiful, the swift of foot—and snaps it short with a laugh. But the gray, fraying, knotted thread? The worthless scrap? That she drags out, mile after bloody mile, through winter after winter, until the fingers grow too stiff to hold the spindle.

There is no sense to it. No justice in the steel. The coward hides behind the baggage-wain and lives to rot of the lung-rot at seventy; the hero leaps into the shield-wall and finds an ash-spear through his gullet before his first child is born. 

Where is the horse now? Where is the rider? Where is the giving of treasure? The high joy of the mead-hall has turned to silent ice. The timber pillars of our glory are eaten by worms, and the songs of the *scop* are lost in the howling of the wind outside these turf walls.

*(She sits back, her posture slumping, releasing a long, shuddering sigh. She tosses the piece of mail into the cold ashes.)*

Let the wind howl. Let the darkness come in. 

I do not fear the shadow-walker. I have lived long enough to know that life is merely a brief warmth between two vast coldnesses. My kin call to me from the barrow-mounds. I hear them in the rustle of the dry leaves; I hear them in the groan of the frozen lake. They ask me why I tarry.

I have no answer for them. I have no answer for *Wyrd*. 

The fire dies. The hall grows dim. Come then, dark weaver. The thread is worn to dust. Cut it… and let the old woman sleep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a poetic monologue in the style of a dark, archaic lament about the transience of human life, the loss of protectors, and the futility of witchcraft.
counterfactuals.output:
Behold the ash, ye children of the fading dusk, and know the measure of your fleeting hour. We are but breath drawn upon a wintered glass, a phantom flicker ere the candle yields unto the hungry dark. 

Where now are the iron-girt lords who swore to stand against the night? Where sleep the hearth-keepers, the great wardens of our youth? Gone, all gone. Their shields are eaten by the worm-red rust; their names are swallowed by the silent clay. The high towers fall to thistles, and the guardians who once held the breach now lay down their crowns to rot beside the churl and the beggar. No trumpet calls them back from the sepulchral sleep. The shield-wall is broken, and we are left naked to the storm.

And I… oh, I have sought to bind the shadow. I have drawn the circle in the marrow-cold earth and whispered to the old, unpitying gods. I brewed the bitter nightshade; I carved the elder runes upon bone and copper, believing that blood and chant might turn the scythe of Time. 

What folly! What wretched, blind conceit! 

My spells are but smoke cast against a gale. The blackest craft cannot mend the snapped thread, nor can the sharpest incantation summon back the soul once the grey river hath claimed it. The potion curdles in the cup; the runes turn to dust beneath my weeping eyes. All our art—our secret names, our turnings of the moon, our sacrifices upon the altar of cold stone—is but a child’s rattle clattered against the thunder. Magic is a lying mirror, reflecting only our own dread back upon us. It saves no king; it spares no witch.

The earth is a graveyard that devours its own offspring, and even the stars grow pale with weariness. Unbind the charms. Let the embers die. For Fate holds no mercy for the carved root or the whispered prayer, and the end comes alike for the hero, the kingdom, and the spell.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a historical fiction scene where an old woman named Ana speaks to a weeping young widow (*wifcynn*) after their lord's death, using Anglo-Saxon imagery like shooting stars, battered swords, and sparrows exiting the feast hall.
counterfactuals.output:
The fire in the great hall was dying, shrinking to a mound of red embers that cast long, shivering shadows against the timber walls. Outside, the winter gale howled across the fen, but inside, the only sound was the muffled, rhythmic sobbing of the young widow. She sat crouched on the rushes, her golden hair unbound, weeping for the lord whose body now lay cold beneath the earth.

Old Ana shifted her heavy wool mantle and stepped softly across the hall. Her hands, gnarled and scarred by decades of salt-work and hearth-fires, rested gently upon the girl’s trembling shoulders. 

"Dry your tears, child of the *wifcynn*," Ana murmured, her voice like the scraping of dry rushes. "You weep as if the world itself has broken, but the weave of *Wyrd* goes on, unravelling and spinning anew."

 The widow pressed her face into her hands, her frame shaking. "He was my sun, Ana. My warmth. Now there is only darkness."

Ana reached out and lifted the girl’s chin, forcing her tear-stained eyes to meet hers. With her free hand, the old woman pointed up toward the high rafters, where their lord’s wargear hung suspended above the hearth. 

"Look there," Ana said softly. "Look at his blade. It is not the polished trinket of a boy playing at war. The iron is notched, the edge battered and bruised from a hundred shield-clashes. It bore the weight of fell strokes; it bit through bone and cracked oak until its work was finished. Would you ask a beaten sword to stay forever in the fray, or would you let it rest upon the wall, its honor proven?"

The young woman looked up, her breath catching as the dim firelight caught the pitted steel of her husband’s sword. 

"Last night, before the hearth went cold," Ana continued, her gaze turning toward the smoke-hole in the roof, "I looked into the black vault of the sky. I saw a shooting star—a streak of white fire that tore through the void. It flamed so fiercely it turned the clouds to silver, and then, in a heartbeat, it was gone, swallowed by the deep night. Such was his life, my child. Short, bright, and burning with a glory that left us all breathless. It is not a tragedy that the fire fell; it is a wonder that we were spared to see it burn."

Ana leaned down, wrapping her rough arms around the weeping widow, pulling the girl’s head against her chest. 

"Remember the old tale," Ana whispered, her breath warm against the young woman’s ear. "This life of ours is no more than the flight of a sparrow through the king’s feast-hall in the depths of winter. Outside, the snow falls and the storm rages. Within, the hall is warm, lit by torches and filled with the scent of mead. The sparrow flies in through one door, flitters for a brief, sweet moment in the warmth, and then passes out through the far door, back into the freezing dark."

Ana stroked the girl’s hair as the girl's quieted sobs slowed to soft gasps. 

"Your lord has only flown out into the dark, little one of the *wifcynn*. He knew the warmth of the hall, and he knew your love. The storm outside belongs to God, but the memory of his flight is ours to keep."
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

Look ye upon these darkling stones, whiles the cauld wind bloweth through the roofless nave. Time, that unsparing churl, eateth the work of giants; naught abideth under the turn of the heavens. Where once the hearth-fire burned red and the brave drank deep of the sweet mead, a grim *wyrdstaef* was carved in secret upon the lintel. Now the high walls stand *gehrorene*, broken by the frost-shatter and smothered in gray moss, and the ring-adorned lords who sang of triumph—they *flet ofgeāfon*, leaving the hall-floor forever to the shadow and the rain. Yea, the glory of this earth withereth like winter-grass, and all the pomp of men is swallowed by the quiet gloom.

Hwœr cōm the steed? Hwœr cōm the rider? Hwœr cōm the giver of treasure? Hwœr cōm the seats of the banquet, and where the hall-joys of old? All hath passed away beneath the night-helm, as though it had never been.
